source.title: High-dimensional Analysis of Knowledge Distillation: Weak-to-Strong Generalization and Scaling Laws
source.authors: M. E. Ildiz; Halil Alperen Gozeten; Ege Onur Taga; Marco Mondelli; Samet Oymak

record.tranche_reason: Extends scaling-law analysis to high-dimensional linear regression and knowledge distillation, rather than language-model pretraining.
record.gate_note: The study reports theoretical and experimental excess test-risk scaling in linear regression, which bears on scaling-law behavior in another training regime. It does not measure language-model cross-entropy, downstream-task performance, or a compute-optimal parameter/token split. The CIFAR-10 accuracy experiment is not a scaling-law result. Results cited from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study derives and simulates excess-risk scaling for ridgeless linear regression whose covariance and signal spectra are assumed to follow power laws. No language model or neural network is scaled. The only neural experiment (CIFAR-10 ResNet-50) is not a scaling result. The power-law form follows from the assumed spectra rather than being an empirical test of loss scaling in any modality or training regime. The finding concerns whether distillation changes the exponent, which no version names, so the scaling results go under fits_no_version rather than testing V5 or V7.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct, with three additions. The optimal surrogate strictly improves risk unless the covariance is isotropic, and only in the over-parameterized regime; there is no gain when n > p. A masked (weak) surrogate that drops tail features can beat training on true labels. The authors attribute the loss of log-log linearity as n approaches p to their asymptotic approximations requiring p ≫ n, not to a genuine bend in the scaling law.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes ridgeless high-dimensional regression and distillation risk, with theoretical asymptotics and synthetic experiments; it does not use language-model pretraining or the original studies' model/token/compute sweeps.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported power-law regimes depend on the eigenvalue and signal decay exponents and the relation between n and p; log-log linearity weakens as n approaches p.

fits_no_version.finding: In ridgeless linear regression with power-law eigenvalues and signal, training on labels from an optimal (or optimally masked) surrogate lowers excess risk but leaves the data-scaling exponent unchanged: Θ(n^-(β−1)) or Θ(n^-2α). Synthetic experiments agree with the theory when p ≫ n.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Knowledge distillation or weak-to-strong training can lower test risk at fixed data but cannot improve the exponent of the data scaling law.

record.problems: The scaling results are for linear-regression excess test risk, not language-model cross-entropy. The stated theoretical scaling assumes power-law eigenvalues and signal coefficients and specifies a noise-variance condition. Experimental trend descriptions are qualitative; the text provides no individual plotted values or uncertainty estimates.
record.rows_left_out: No other reported results were omitted for the tested versions. The CIFAR-10 accuracy experiment and Figure 2b's theory-versus-experiment comparison were excluded because they do not report a scaling-law result bearing on the claim versions.

untested.parts: No language-model pretraining loss scaling in parameters, tokens or compute.
No extrapolation from small to large runs.
No empirical scaling in other modalities, data repetition, fine-tuning or transfer for neural models. The linear-regression power laws follow from assumed spectra.
No comparison of fitted exponents across setups or fitting methods in trained models. The departures near n≈p are artifacts of the asymptotic approximation.

record.verdict_notes: This is a theoretical stat.ML paper on distillation in linear regression; its scaling results hold by construction from assumed power-law spectra. The reader's V5 and V7 labels are removed. The CIFAR-10 experiment reports accuracy over epochs only and has no scaling content.

versions.untested_parts: No language models, held-out pretraining cross-entropy, or scaling in parameters, tokens, or compute.
No extrapolation from small runs to much larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation between model parameters and training tokens.
No comparison of depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
Tests excess test-risk scaling in linear regression and distillation, not other modalities or language-model pretraining loss.
No downstream-task performance or its relationship to pretraining loss.
Does not compare fitted exponents or compute-optimal splits across fitting methods, parameter-count conventions, schedules, or datasets.

rows.subject: ridgeless over-parameterized linear regression with optimal surrogate parameter βs*
rows.operation_detail: Theoretical excess test-risk scaling with sample size n under the optimal surrogate parameter.

conditions.value: σt² = O(n^-γ), where γ is the noiseless scaling exponent

rows.measure: Asymptotic excess test risk as a function of sample size n
rows.note: The theorem states that the optimal-surrogate risk has the same scaling as the standard target risk under the specified power-law assumptions.
rows.check: Theoretical derivation (Prop. 6) for linear regression under assumed power-law spectra. It is not a measured scaling of a neural or language model, and the power law is built into the assumptions. It bears on the distillation-exponent finding, not on V5.

rows.subject: optimal surrogate models and standard target model in linear regression
rows.operation_detail: Test risks plotted against sample size; the text describes the log-log trend and its departure near p.
rows.baseline: Standard target risk is plotted alongside the optimal masked-surrogate and optimal-surrogate risks
rows.value: A linear trend is observable for smaller n; it is less apparent as n approaches p due to finite-sample effects.
rows.note: The text describes the plotted trend but gives no individual risk values.
rows.check: Synthetic linear-regression check of the theory (Fig. 4a, p=500). The authors attribute the loss of linearity near p to the asymptotic approximation needing p ≫ n. That is a finite-dimension artifact of the toy model, not curves bending in trained models, so it is not V7 evidence. The 'partial' state has no version to refer to.

rows.subject: optimal surrogate models and standard target model in linear regression
rows.operation_detail: Test risks plotted against sample size in log-log scale.
rows.baseline: Standard target risk is plotted alongside the optimal masked-surrogate and optimal-surrogate risks
rows.value: The text reports clear linear behavior in the log-log plot, consistent with the scaling-law result.
rows.note: The text describes the plotted trend but gives no individual risk values.
rows.check: Synthetic validation of the theory at p=5000 (Fig. 4b). It is not a scaling measurement on any system the versions name.

rows.subject: two-stage linear regression model
rows.operation_detail: Experimental test risk plotted against sample size with surrogate and target sample sizes set equal.
rows.measure: Test risk versus sample size in log-log scale
rows.value: The text reports similar linear behavior when m = n is sufficiently small relative to p; linearity disappears as m = n approaches p.
rows.note: The statement aggregates the four listed α settings; individual risk values are not given in the text.
rows.check: Fig. 5 compares theoretical and experimental two-stage risk in a synthetic setting. α=0.5 and α=1 fall outside the α>1 assumption of Props. 4–7. The deviation near p is again attributed to the asymptotic approximation. Not V5 or V7 evidence.
